dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: AI writing: Present gains can weaken future judgment
st.an: The source accepts supervised, selective AI augmentation and materially develops the cluster’s proposition by explaining how opaque output can make verification impractical while delegation removes opportunities to build the judgment needed for oversight. Its evidence is chiefly expert personal observation and a confirmed case study, not proof of general or durable deskilling.
qs: Sometimes the AI's work is so sophisticated that you couldn't check it if you tried.

And that suggests another risk we don't talk about enough: every time we hand work to a wizard, we lose a chance to develop our own expertise, to build the very judgment we need to evaluate the wizard's work.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source directly supports selective, task-specific deployment: it describes AI capability as jagged, reports impressive but non-generalizable results, and emphasizes that opaque agentic work can make verification costly or impossible. It also reinforces the need to preserve human expertise and choose deliberately among delegation, collaboration and no AI.
qs: This emphasizes the jagged frontier of AI: it is very good at some things and worse at others in ways that are hard to predict without experience.
Sometimes the AI's work is so sophisticated that you couldn't check it if you tried.

kp.k: AI collaboration is shifting toward opaque autonomous delegation
kp.d: Mollick argues that recent AI systems increasingly produce sophisticated work from vague requests without human participation in the process. This is a cross-domain argument about changing human–AI relationships, not a finding specifically about legal services. He contrasts collaborative co-intelligence with receiving outputs from a largely opaque 'wizard', while maintaining that collaboration remains important.
qs: We're moving from partners to audience, from collaboration to conjuring.
We're shifting from being collaborators who shape the process to being supplicants who receive the output.

kp.k: NotebookLM illustrates useful synthesis requiring retrospective fact-checking
kp.d: Mollick reports feeding his book and all 140 or so One Useful Thing posts into NotebookLM to generate a video overview. After reviewing it several times, he found the numerical claims correct and no substantive errors, but identified incomplete attribution of his co-authored study and presentation choices he disliked. This is a personal demonstration, not a systematic accuracy evaluation; he remained unable to explain how the system selected its content.
qs: So, I went through the video several times, checking all the facts.
Also, I wouldn't have said everything the way the AI did (it was a little bombastic, and my book is not out-of-date yet!), but there were no substantive errors.

kp.k: GPT-5 Pro found an overlooked academic paper error
kp.d: In Mollick's account, GPT-5 Pro critiqued his previously peer-reviewed job market paper in nine minutes and forty seconds, apparently using code, Monte Carlo analysis and reinterpretation of fixed effects. It identified a minor error linking numbers across two tables that prior readers had missed. Mollick checked the results and found them correct, but could not establish whether all claimed analytical procedures actually occurred. His positive experience is explicitly qualified by possible undiscovered errors and failures on other tasks.
qs: Nine minutes and forty seconds later, I had a very detailed critique.
The error involved two different sets of numbers in two tables that were linked in ways I did not explicitly spell out in my paper.
I checked through the results, and found that it was, but I still have no idea of what the AI did to discover this problem, nor whether the other things it claimed to have done happened as described.
I haven't found an error yet, but that doesn't mean there aren't any.

kp.k: Claude transformed financial teaching materials with limited instruction
kp.d: Mollick reports that Claude 4.1 Opus converted a multi-tab financial-model exercise about desk manufacturing into a cheese-shop exercise after one instruction, reading the lesson plan and formulas and producing a new spreadsheet within minutes. His review found that it preserved the teaching objective, with formula and modelling choices he regarded mainly as differences of opinion. A subsequent pitch deck was a solid start without major errors but not ready for use, illustrating uneven capabilities rather than universal task competence.
qs: A few minutes later, with just the one prompt, I had a new, transformed spreadsheet downloaded on my computer, one that had entirely new data while still communicating the key lesson.
This is a pretty solid start to a pitch deck, and one without any major errors, but it also isn't ready-to-go.
This emphasizes the jagged frontier of AI: it is very good at some things and worse at others in ways that are hard to predict without experience.

kp.k: Agents plan, execute and self-correct without user-selected steps
kp.d: Mollick characterises these systems as agents that autonomously pursue goals. In the spreadsheet example, Claude planned and executed the work, fixed the spreadsheet twice without being asked and checked its answers repeatedly. He attributes the lack of externally selected steps to reinforcement-learning-powered agents learning their own approaches, distinguishing this workflow from interactive human guidance.
qs: These new AI systems are essentially agents, AI that can plan and act autonomously toward given goals.
But it also adjusted to unexpected errors, twice fixing the spreadsheet (without me asking) and verifying its answers multiple times.

kp.k: Process summaries cannot establish what an agent actually did
kp.d: Mollick argues that reported steps offer limited transparency: Claude supplies summaries, GPT-5 Pro offers less information and NotebookLM almost none. Even fuller disclosure would require expertise spanning the task's component fields. He separately identifies factual correctness and judgement about framing as concerns that users may struggle to address when they cannot intervene.
qs: Not only can I not intervene, I also cannot be entirely sure what the AI system actually did.
The steps that Claude reported are mere summaries of its work, GPT-5 Pro provides even less information, while NotebookLM gives you almost no insights at all into its process in creating a video.
And even if the facts are right, maybe I would have made a different judgement about how to present or frame them.

kp.k: Verification can offset or exceed production time savings
kp.d: Mollick compares the outputs in his examples to work expected from a graduate student over a couple of hours or more, delivered instead in minutes. However, he stresses that expertise and favourable initial review do not establish that every detail is error-free. Human checking can take less time than doing the task, more time, or exceed the user's ability altogether; the productivity comparison is his assessment of these examples, not a measured general result.
qs: They are what I would expect from a graduate student working for a couple hours (or more, in the case of the re-analysis of my paper), except I got them in minutes.
Of course, I can't actually tell you if the documents are error-free without checking every detail.
Sometimes that takes far less time than doing the work yourself, sometimes it takes a lot more.
Sometimes the AI's work is so sophisticated that you couldn't check it if you tried.

kp.k: Delegation risks eroding expertise needed to judge outputs
kp.d: Mollick identifies a formation problem: outsourcing work removes opportunities to develop the judgement required to evaluate that work. He presents this as a risk and an urgent educational challenge, rather than reporting measured skill deterioration. The dilemma is how to teach verification in fields learners have not mastered while AI use may impede the acquisition of mastery.
qs: And that suggests another risk we don't talk about enough: every time we hand work to a wizard, we lose a chance to develop our own expertise, to build the very judgment we need to evaluate the wizard's work.
This creates a hard problem for education: How do you train someone to verify work in fields they haven't mastered, when the AI itself prevents them from developing mastery?

kp.k: New literacy requires choosing appropriate human–AI working modes
kp.d: Mollick recommends learning when to delegate autonomously, when to collaborate iteratively and when not to use AI. He emphasises continuing human advantages where AI falls short and the frequent superiority of back-and-forth collaboration over an unaided machine. He also recommends cultivating experience-based judgement about outputs, including when failure or uncertainty makes reliance inappropriate.
qs: First, learn when to summon the wizard versus when to work with AI as a co-intelligence or to not use AI at all.
But for the increasing number of tasks where AI is useful, co-intelligence, and the back-and-forth it requires, is often superior to a machine alone.
We need to curate and select among the outputs the AI provides, but more than that, we need to work with AI enough to develop instincts for when it succeeds and when it fails.

kp.k: Provisional trust prioritises usefulness when complete verification becomes impossible
kp.d: Mollick recommends purpose-sensitive provisional trust rather than requiring complete certainty for every output. He distinguishes complex AI work from familiar technological delegation: research or spreadsheet errors may be harder to detect than a bad GPS route or entertainment recommendation. His concluding argument is that growing competence accompanies opacity, with the greatest need for assistance arising precisely where users are least able to verify it.
qs: Finally, embrace provisional trust.
The wizard model means working with "good enough" more often, not because we're lowering standards, but because perfect verification is becoming impossible.
The question isn't "Is this completely correct?" but "Is this useful enough for this purpose?"
The paradox of working with AI wizards is that competence and opacity rise together.
We need these tools most for the tasks where we're least able to verify them.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Mollick claims that increasingly autonomous AI is shifting knowledge work from human–AI collaboration toward delegated production followed by human verification.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain account of research, teaching-material preparation and business-document production, not a claim specifically about legal services. Mollick describes agents that plan, execute and adjust multi-step work from minimal instructions, producing sophisticated outputs while giving users less influence over, or visibility into, the process. He argues that users increasingly become recipients and judges of finished work rather than collaborators in its production.

pts.k: Mollick claims that selected complex tasks can now be completed in minutes at a quality comparable to hours or more of graduate-student work, including detecting a previously unnoticed research error.
pts.d: He reports that NotebookLM produced a useful video synthesis of his writing, GPT-5 Pro critiqued his published research and identified a small linked-table error, and Claude 4.1 Opus transformed a teaching spreadsheet into a new business context. These are claims about particular observed outputs, not measured profession-wide productivity gains. His account distinguishes the research error he checked from the model's claimed experimental procedures, which he could not fully confirm.

pts.k: Mollick argues that sophisticated AI output creates a verification burden that can erase time savings or exceed users' expertise, while delegation can weaken the development of that expertise.
pts.d: He distinguishes apparently correct facts from acceptable judgment, framing and presentation. He claims that even access to process descriptions would not necessarily enable users to assess work spanning multiple specialties. He also identifies a learning risk: handing tasks to AI removes practice through which people develop the judgment needed to check future outputs. His broader claim is that rising competence and opacity make errors harder to detect, particularly in tasks where users most need assistance.

pts.k: Mollick proposes a new working literacy based on choosing when to delegate, judging outputs and using purpose-dependent provisional trust.
pts.d: His prescription is not universal autonomous substitution. Users should choose among unaided human work, collaborative AI use and more autonomous delegation. He argues that experience with AI is needed to recognize success and failure, and that some work will require acceptance of useful-enough output without complete verification. This is a recommendation and anticipated adaptation, rather than an empirically established standard for safe reliance.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists principally of Mollick's firsthand trials and expert checking of selected outputs; the wider workflow and learning claims are interpretations of those experiences.
pts.d: For NotebookLM, he supplied his book and approximately 140 posts, then repeatedly watched and checked the resulting video. He reports correct numbers and no substantive errors, while noting incomplete attribution and stylistic reservations. The references to MMLU and neurosurgery-exam data concern facts reproduced in that video, not new benchmark tests conducted in this article. For GPT-5 Pro, he reports a critique returned in nine minutes and forty seconds and confirmation of a previously unnoticed error; he explicitly does not confirm that all reported analyses occurred as described. For Claude, he inspected the transformed spreadsheet and found it preserved the teaching lesson, with some modeling and formula choices he would change; its pitch deck was a useful start, not ready to use. The source supplies no systematic error-rate, productivity or longitudinal learning study for its broader claims.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The source describes a shift already emerging in 2025 and extending to work more broadly in the near term, without a dated forecast or claim of universal capability.
pts.d: Mollick says his view changed over the preceding few weeks. His examples depend on then-current capabilities, including paid access to GPT-5 Pro and Claude's recently introduced file-working features. Expansion is qualified by the unpredictable 'jagged frontier': success on one task does not establish success on another. He acknowledges undetected errors, outright failure on other tasks and the continuing superiority of human work or collaborative AI use in appropriate situations. Provisional trust is framed as dependent on the output's purpose, not complete correctness.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly illustrated users are researchers and educators; the broader implications concern knowledge workers, learners and those responsible for training them.
pts.d: Researchers gain rapid critique and reanalysis but must assess methods and results they may not be able to reconstruct. Educators can rapidly adapt financial-model exercises and teaching content; business-document users can obtain spreadsheets and draft pitch decks, though not necessarily finished deliverables. Knowledge workers increasingly select and verify outputs rather than shape every production step. Learners risk losing opportunities to build expertise, while educators face the problem of teaching verification before mastery. Graduate students appear as a comparison for work quality and time, not as evidence of measured job displacement. The article identifies no specific effects on lawyers, law firms, legal clients or legal markets.
